kid.question: What danger does Ebed-melech report about Jeremiah?

options.text: He may drown in water
He may be sold abroad
He may die of hunger
He may fall from the wall

kid.explanation: Ebed-melech tells the king that Jeremiah is likely to die of hunger in the dungeon.

kid.question: What does Ebed-melech send down to protect Jeremiah under the ropes?

options.text: Old cloths from the royal house
Fresh branches from the palace garden
Woven mats from the temple court
Leather belts from the city guards

kid.explanation: Ebed-melech lowers old cloths and rags and tells Jeremiah to put them under his arms beneath the cords.

kid.question: Where does Jeremiah stay after being lifted out?

options.text: In the home of Ebed-melech
In a camp beside the river
In the chamber of the priests
In the court of the prison

kid.explanation: Jeremiah is drawn up with cords and remains in the prison court.

kid.question: What does Jeremiah tell the king to do to stay alive?

options.text: Wait inside the temple gates
Go out to Babylon's officials
Send his soldiers toward Egypt
Hide his family outside Jerusalem

kid.explanation: The message promises life to Zedekiah and his household if he goes out to the Babylonian princes.

kid.question: Who does Zedekiah fear will mock him?

options.text: The priests who read the scroll
The Egyptians who left the city
The Jews who joined the Chaldeans
The children who live in Benjamin

kid.explanation: Zedekiah says he fears being handed over to Jews who have gone over to the Chaldeans and being mocked.

kid.question: What happens when Zedekiah tries to escape?

options.text: He is caught near Jericho
He is welcomed into Egypt
He is hidden near Anathoth
He is crowned again in Judah

kid.explanation: Zedekiah flees by night, but the Chaldean army overtakes him in the plains of Jericho.

kid.question: What do the Chaldeans do to Jerusalem's walls?

options.text: They build the walls higher
They paint the walls white
They line the walls with tents
They break the walls down

kid.explanation: The Chaldeans burn houses and break down Jerusalem's walls.

kid.question: What is given to poor people left in Judah?

options.text: Horses and chariots to drive
Vineyards and fields to use
Silver and gold to trade
Weapons and armor to carry

kid.explanation: The captain leaves some poor people in Judah and gives them vineyards and fields.

kid.question: Why does the Lord promise to save Ebed-melech?

options.text: Because he has trusted in Him
Because he has paid the captors
Because he has fled to Egypt
Because he has joined the army

kid.explanation: God promises Ebed-melech his life because he put his trust in the Lord.

kid.question: What family image describes the lonely city?

options.text: A child separated from his parents
A woman who has lost her husband
A father grieving for his child
A brother left behind by his family

kid.explanation: The once-populous city is pictured as solitary and like a widow.

high-school.question: How does Ebed-melech's rescue combine advocacy with practical care?

options.text: He pays the jailers and escorts Jeremiah directly to his family home
He names the danger and cushions the ropes used to lift Jeremiah
He confronts the captors and gives Jeremiah armor for his escape
He requests a hearing and prepares Jeremiah to answer the officials

high-school.explanation: Ebed-melech calls the officials' act evil and reports the hunger danger, then uses cloths under the ropes in the rescue.

high-school.question: Why does Jeremiah hesitate when Zedekiah asks for a full answer?

options.text: He lacks a message and doubts the king has authority to ask
He plans to escape and doubts the guards will let him return
He fears Babylon and doubts the Chaldeans will honor their agreement
He fears being killed and doubts the king will follow his counsel

high-school.explanation: Jeremiah asks whether the king will kill him if he speaks and whether the king will listen to his counsel.

high-school.question: What determines the two futures Jeremiah sets before Zedekiah?

options.text: Whether he goes out to the Babylonian officials
Whether he sends a larger tribute to Egypt
Whether he releases the remaining temple prisoners
Whether he gathers the city's soldiers at the gate

high-school.explanation: Going out means life and an unburned city; refusing means capture and burning.

high-school.question: How does Jeremiah address the king's stated fear?

options.text: He promises a successful escape through the king's garden
He advises secrecy so the Chaldeans cannot identify him
He denies the feared handover and urges obedience for life
He recommends sending the Jews back into Jerusalem

high-school.explanation: Zedekiah fears mockery by defectors; Jeremiah says they will not receive him and urges him to obey the Lord and live.

high-school.question: How is the private conversation handled afterward?

options.text: The king announces it publicly and the officials approve its terms
Jeremiah writes it on a scroll and sends it to Babylon
The king orders secrecy and Jeremiah gives the prescribed account
Jeremiah denies meeting the king and leaves the prison court

high-school.explanation: The king instructs Jeremiah to report his request not to return to Jonathan's house; the officials leave off questioning him.

high-school.question: How does Zedekiah's escape attempt relate to the warning he received?

options.text: He secures freedom and the city survives under his successor
He is captured and the city burns despite his flight
He reaches Egypt and gains soldiers to retake the city
He remains hidden while the conquerors restore Jerusalem's walls

high-school.explanation: His flight ends in capture, judgment, blinding, and chains; the Chaldeans burn houses and break the walls.

high-school.question: What distinction is made among the people after Jerusalem falls?

options.text: Many are deported while some poor people remain with land
The wealthy remain while the poor are sent to Babylon
The soldiers remain while the farmers are sent to Egypt
The priests depart while the foreign merchants inherit the city

high-school.explanation: The captain carries away remaining people and defectors, but leaves some poor people and gives them vineyards and fields.

high-school.question: How is Jeremiah treated under the Babylonian order?

options.text: He is punished and sent in chains to the king's prison
He is appointed to command the remaining Babylonian soldiers
He is ordered to replace the temple officials who opposed him
He is protected and released to dwell among the people

high-school.explanation: Nebuchadrezzar orders care and no harm for Jeremiah, who is brought from the prison court and entrusted to Gedaliah.

high-school.question: How does Ebed-melech's promise fit the city's announced disaster?

options.text: God cancels the judgment because Ebed-melech has served the king
God promises him rule over the people captured by Babylon
God distinguishes his personal deliverance within the coming judgment
God sends him to Egypt before allowing the siege to begin

high-school.explanation: The Lord affirms that His words against the city will occur but promises Ebed-melech deliverance and life because he trusted Him.

high-school.question: How do the opening images portray Jerusalem's reversal?

options.text: A crowded and honored city becomes lonely, dependent, and without comfort
A small and ignored village becomes a center for worship and commerce
A fortified royal camp becomes the home of returning pilgrims and priests
A foreign-controlled city becomes prosperous through stronger regional alliances

high-school.explanation: The city once full and princely is now solitary, like a widow, tributary, betrayed, and deprived of festival attendance.

expert.question: How is responsibility distributed through the rescue of Jeremiah?

options.text: The king identifies the danger, the officials command rescue, and Ebed-melech frees Jeremiah
Jeremiah requests release, the king refuses permission, and servants secretly lift him
The guards report danger, Ebed-melech orders release, and the king approves it afterward
Ebed-melech identifies the danger, the king authorizes rescue, and men lift Jeremiah

expert.explanation: Ebed-melech reports the danger to the king, receives authorization to take men, gathers protective cloths, and directs the lifting of Jeremiah.

expert.question: What distinction remains after the king swears to preserve Jeremiah's life?

options.text: Protection for the speaker requires the withdrawal of the warning to the city
The king's oath guarantees that Babylon will abandon the siege without surrender
Protection for the speaker does not settle the hearer's response to his counsel
The king's oath replaces the conditional message with unconditional royal safety

expert.explanation: The oath addresses Jeremiah's fear of death, but Jeremiah still presents outcomes dependent on Zedekiah's going out or refusing.

expert.question: How does the warning challenge the king's effort to avoid humiliation?

options.text: Refusal risks captivity and reproach rather than securing the honor he fears losing
Refusal secures honor for the king while exposing only his household to captivity
Surrender guarantees mockery by defectors while leaving the city untouched by fire
Surrender requires humiliation by Egypt before Babylon will accept the king's household

expert.explanation: Jeremiah counters the feared handover, then describes refusal leading to capture, family loss, and women's reproach about misleading friends.

expert.question: What does the account distinguish between the private counsel and the official inquiry?

options.text: The inquiry receives the surrender counsel and orders the king to follow it immediately
The inquiry receives a permitted account of a petition rather than the surrender counsel
The inquiry receives a written version of the king's oath and releases the prophet
The inquiry reveals the king's conversation and results in renewed confinement in mire

expert.explanation: The officials hear the account the king prescribed about not returning to Jonathan's house; the private matter is not discovered.

expert.question: How does the fate of Zedekiah answer the alternatives of the earlier private oracle?

options.text: Flight fails to prevent capture or the burning announced for refusal to surrender
Flight secures the life and unburned city promised for going to Babylon's officials
His capture is followed by the city's preservation under the same royal household
His capture reverses the warning because the Chaldeans accept him as their ruler

expert.explanation: Zedekiah attempts flight rather than the described going out, is captured, and the houses burn as the warning anticipated.

expert.question: What social reversal accompanies the deportations?

options.text: People who had nothing finance the deportation by selling their ancestral estates
Former royal officials receive the estates of poor families deported to Babylon
People who had nothing receive productive land while others are carried away
Former royal officials remain in charge of the city while their workers escape

expert.explanation: The captain leaves some of the poor who had nothing and gives them vineyards and fields as others are deported.

expert.question: What contrast emerges between Jeremiah's confinement and the conqueror's instructions?

options.text: The imprisoned prophet receives the punishment previously reserved for Zedekiah's officers
The imprisoned prophet receives an explicit order of protection and considerate treatment
The conqueror preserves the prophet's confinement as proof of the officials' authority
The conqueror commands the prophet to recant before releasing him to Gedaliah

expert.explanation: Nebuchadrezzar orders that Jeremiah be cared for and unharmed, and he is removed from the prison court to dwell among the people.

expert.question: What is the temporal placement of the promise to Ebed-melech?

options.text: It was spoken after Ebed-melech became ruler and before Jeremiah entered confinement
It was spoken during the rebuilding of Jerusalem and reported before the siege began
It was spoken after the city's return from captivity and reported as a new warning
It was spoken during Jeremiah's confinement and reported amid the fall's aftermath

expert.explanation: The narrative explicitly dates this word to Jeremiah's confinement, although it recounts it after the city's fall and Jeremiah's release.

expert.question: What does the promise identify as the basis and extent of Ebed-melech's exception?

options.text: Service in the royal household grounds inheritance of Zedekiah's vacant throne
Trust in the Lord grounds preservation of his life amid fulfilled judgment
Military aid to Babylon grounds permanent exemption from every future danger
Knowledge of the escape route grounds rescue of the entire royal household

expert.explanation: The Lord says the city's judgment will occur, yet Ebed-melech will not fall by the sword and will retain his life because he trusted Him.

expert.question: How do personification and abandoned worship routes reinforce one another?

options.text: The grieving city's isolation is embodied in empty approaches to its solemn feasts
The grieving city's recovery is embodied in returning crowds at its solemn feasts
The widowed city replaces worship with tribute that restores its former friendships
The widowed city gains rest through the departure of those who formerly attended worship

expert.explanation: The city weeps without comfort, while Zion's ways mourn because no one comes to the solemn feasts and its gates are desolate.
